item.title: Play Console DEX optimization and an R8 keep rule – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Measurement

Play Console said our DEX was 39% optimized. The culprit was a keep rule for an SDK we never used

A leftover Kakao SDK ProGuard file kept every public member of every class out of R8; deleting it moved the bundle's r8.json numbers from 39% to 85%.

Play Console still rated the latest bundle of SugarSpeller, our Korean spelling checker, as "intermediate" on September 25, 2026: optimization 36%, obfuscation 39%, shrinking 39%. Five days earlier we had removed the -dontoptimize line that kept R8 from optimizing at all. The rest of the gap came from one seven-line ProGuard file for the Kakao SDK, which the app does not use. With it gone the same day, the unshrunk share in the bundle's r8.json fell from 61.47% to 15.18% (85% once subtracted from 100), and the AAB went from 18.4 MB to 11.6 MB.

Numbers come from SugarMount's app repository (sugarspeller): commits a597223 (2026-09-20) and e05f8e3 (2026-09-25), the changelog entries for 1.6.020 and 1.6.023, the post-release watch log, and an r8.json read again from a local release AAB while writing this note. Checked on October 20, 2026.

The Play Console figure is r8.json turned upside down

Those percentages line up with a file the Android Gradle Plugin (AGP) already puts in every R8-processed release bundle: BUNDLE-METADATA/com.android.tools/r8.json. Its stats block records the share of code that was not shrunk, obfuscated or optimized.

unzip -p app-release.aab BUNDLE-METADATA/com.android.tools/r8.json
"stats":{"noObfuscationPercentage":61.48,
         "noOptimizationPercentage":64.27,
         "noShrinkingPercentage":61.47}

Subtract each value from 100 and you get what Play shows: 61.47 became 39% shrunk, 64.27 became 36% optimized. We matched that from our own before-and-after numbers, not from a Google spec, but it held for the two Play readings we have (0% before, 36/39/39% after the first fix). The practical upshot is that you can read the metric locally before uploading anything.

The build used AGP 9.4.0 with R8 full mode, resource shrinking and the stock proguard-android-optimize.txt. Our repository notes say Play wants this metric addressed by February 2027; we could not re-check the wording on the Play screen for this note.

Dropping -dontoptimize took optimization from 0% to 36%

Commit a597223 on September 20 removed -dontoptimize from proguard-common.pro. It had been added on purpose, out of fear that optimization would break the Gson reflection that parses spelling results, and it pinned Play's optimization figure at 0%. The comparison baseline was the previous HEAD (1.6.019) built in the same environment.

Unoptimized code went from 100% to 64.25%, and uncompressed DEX from 16.31 MB to 14.84 MB. The AAB dropped from 29.95 MB to 18.33 MB, but most of that was a greeting-card editor and roughly 11 MB of its assets leaving in the same release. Optimization's own share sits inside the 1.5 MB of DEX.

One number moved the wrong way. Unobfuscated code rose from 54.16% to 61.46%. The commit put that down to "app code shrank, so the SDK keep rules weigh more" and moved on. Version 1.6.020 shipped on September 22. Three days later came the 36/39/39% reading from the top of this note.

The merged configuration.txt had a rule on class *

Every rule R8 actually applied ends up in one file, app/build/outputs/mapping/release/configuration.txt: the defaults, the app's six .pro files, and the consumer rules each library AAR brings along. Reading through it on September 25 turned up this block.

# proguard-kakao.pro (in the repo since the first commit, 2020-12-16)
-keep class com.kakao.** { *; }
-keepattributes Signature
-keepclassmembers class * {
  public static <fields>;
  public *;
}
-dontwarn android.support.v4.**,org.slf4j.**,com.google.android.gms.**

The third rule is the problem. class * has no condition, so it matches every class in the app and in every library. Their public fields and methods can then not be removed, renamed or inlined. And the Kakao SDK (the SDK for KakaoTalk login and sharing) was not a dependency at all; even its Maven repository line in the root build script was commented out.

Commit e05f8e3 deleted the file and both build references to it, release and debug. It also deleted proguard-retrofit2.pro, which no build had ever referenced. (The merged file from the October 9, 2026 release build is 1,369 lines. Short enough to read end to end.)

Do not ship an unconditional keep rule on class * in an Android app. Libraries that need rules already ship them as consumer rules inside their AAR.

Before and after: r8.json and sizes for both changes

Each pair of columns comes from a different day and a different commit, so compare within a pair. Even the same configuration drifts in the second decimal: 64.25% on September 20, 64.27% on September 25.

Metric1.6.019 baseline-dontoptimize removed (Sep 20)Before kakao file removal (Sep 25)After (Sep 25)
Not optimized100%64.25%64.27%15.68%
Not obfuscated54.16%61.46%61.48%15.14%
Not shrunknot recordednot recorded61.47%15.18%
As Play shows it (opt/obf/shrink)optimization 0% (Play screen)36/39/- (derived from r8.json)36/39/39% (Play screen)84/85/85 (derived from r8.json, not yet seen on Play)
DEX16.31 MB (uncompressed)14.84 MB15.6 MB (total)8.2 MB
AAB29.95 MB18.33 MB (asset removal included)18.4 MB11.6 MB

Measured by DEX size, deleting one rule did about five times what removing -dontoptimize did. DEX shrank by 1.5 MB on September 20 and by 7.4 MB (47%) on September 25, and the AAB lost another 6.8 MB.

Before release, a release APK signed with the debug key ran on an API 34 emulator. A spelling check against Naver (Korea's largest web portal) came back with the two corrections the server reported, and the post-check quiz bubble, the quiz screen and Remote Config content injection all worked. The five JSON key strings Gson reads were still present verbatim in the release DEX. (A headless emulator returns black screenshots, so we read screen text with uiautomator dump instead.)

The post-release watch log closes the loop. From September 22 to October 3 it recorded zero crashes for 1.6.020, for 1.6.024 (the first release without the kakao rule) and for 1.6.025, and closed the item as "no regression".

The clue the agent explained away

An AI coding agent (Claude) wrote both commits. On September 20 it declared in the commit message that the -dontoptimize line was the cause. It also recorded, accurately, that unobfuscated code had gone up by more than 7 points. What it did not do was check which rule was holding that code; it filled the gap with a guess that the keep rules had not changed and the SDKs simply weighed more.

A person caught it. On the afternoon of September 25 the operator pasted a Play Console screenshot, noted that the bundle still looked unoptimized, and asked for a deeper analysis. Only then did the agent open the merged configuration, and the seven-line file from 2020 surfaced. Opening configuration.txt first instead of guessing would have saved five days.

Two lines went into the repository's agent instructions afterwards: never add a keep rule on class *, and check the merged result in configuration.txt. The checks we run to catch release-only R8 failures before shipping are in What to check before shipping an AI-built Android app.

Still open

  • Confirming the Play screen. The repository holds only the 85% derived from r8.json; nothing records the Play Console figure after release. We will capture it on the next upload.
  • The ratio creeping back. A new Firebase dependency in 1.6.025 pulled the build down about 5 points, to roughly 80%. The release AAB left on disk from October 9, 2026 reads 20.23% unoptimized with 9.30 MB of DEX (9,302,488 bytes). Next step: diff configuration.txt to see which consumer rule arrived.

FAQ

Does the Play Console DEX optimization warning block uploads?

It did not in September 2026: bundles at 0% and at 36% optimization both shipped normally. Our repository notes say Play expects it fixed by February 2027, so it is not something to leave for later.

Can I see the optimization percentage before uploading to Play?

Yes. Extract BUNDLE-METADATA/com.android.tools/r8.json from the release AAB and subtract the three stats values from 100. For this app, 61.47 matched Play's 39%. That mapping is our inference from repository records, and nothing yet records whether Play showed the 85% that 15.18 implies.

How do I find the keep rule that is holding the metric down?

Search the merged configuration.txt for -keep or -keepclassmembers rules on wide patterns such as class * or ** with no condition attached. Here it was a single -keepclassmembers class * { public *; } block in a file for an SDK the app did not use.

item.title: Accurate sitemap lastmod from a content hash – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Short note

Every sitemap lastmod had the same date: deriving modified dates from a content hash

Don't type lastmod by hand or copy it from git commit dates. Compute it from a hash of the page body, and keep the date itself out of what you hash.

Pull sitemap.xml out of commit 12ed443 and count its lastmod values: every one of the 51 URLs says <lastmod>2026-10-18</lastmod>. One commit earlier there were five different dates. Today a page's modified date only moves when its body hash changes. A commit on October 19 touched 99 HTML files and moved the date on just 6 existing pages.

Sources: this site's git history, tools/dates.py and tools/indexnow.py, checked on October 20, 2026.

Commit dates made every page look new

The old build set each URL's lastmod to the date of the last git commit that touched the file. That helper, git_date, arrived on October 5 in bdbbe97, a commit that carries an AI coding agent's co-author line. The agent's code measured when a file changed. A sitemap needs to know when the content did.

It broke on 12ed443, a site-wide pass. Fifty-two HTML files went into one commit, each gaining an RSS <link> in its head, and all 51 sitemap URLs ended up on that day. Re-running today's hash rule (the inside of <main>) over those 52 files, only 2 had real body changes: the SugarDoc app page in Korean and English. 42 had identical bodies. The other 8 differed by a single added line, a "last updated" date. (Counting structured data in the head as well, 11 pages changed their FAQ or feature list.)

Google's sitemap documentation says it uses lastmod only if the value is "consistently and verifiably" accurate, and gives a copyright date update as an example of a change that isn't significant. Moving 51 dates for one RSS line is how you lose that.

The date moves only when the body hash changes

The October 18 restructure, b82faac, moved all page dates into one file, data/content-dates.json. The agent co-wrote that commit too. What differed was the basis: the new tools/dates.py opens by citing a written spec section for dates (IA spec 4.1). For a hand-written page it hashes the inside of <main> with breadcrumbs and build-generated blocks removed:

def hand_input(page_html):
    inner = main_html(page_html)       # inside <main> only
    inner = _CRUMBS_RE.sub("", inner)  # drop breadcrumbs
    inner = strip_build_blocks(inner)  # drop <!-- build:* --> blocks
    return _WS_RE.sub(" ", inner).strip()
# same hash: keep dates; new hash: modified = today
# new page: published = modified = today

The easy thing to miss is the date itself. In 12ed443 the "last updated" line sat inside <main> as plain HTML. Hash that line and every date change looks like a content change, so the next day's build moves the date again, forever. On hand-written pages the line now lives in a build:meta block. Those 8 app pages became generated pages built from data/apps.json, so their hash covers the input data, not the HTML. A unit test (test_every_marker_block_is_removed) asserts the phrase never reaches the hash input, and test_idempotent_next_day checks that a rerun the next day leaves the dates alone.

Never derive lastmod from commit dates or build dates. Don't let people edit it either: the repository's AGENTS.md says "never edit dates by hand" (how we write that file is in How to write AGENTS.md).

99 files touched, 6 dates moved

Commit b79f2d1 on October 19 touched 99 HTML files, mostly to bump a ?v= cache-busting value on the stylesheet links. Apart from 14 new pages, the modified date moved on 6 existing ones: the home page, the apps hub and the privacy policy list, in Korean and English, each of which now lists the new pages.

IndexNow pings follow the same dates. tools/indexnow.py picks only pages whose modified date is today, and it is a dry run unless you pass --send.

What we check next

The related-notes list (build:extra) is excluded from the hash. Google counts link changes as significant, yet when a new note joins that list, older notes keep their dates. We will decide after reading Search Console's crawl data in November 2026.

FAQ

Does Google actually use sitemap lastmod?

Yes, but only when the values are consistently and verifiably accurate, for example when they match the page's real last change. The same page (updated 2026-07-08) says Google ignores priority and changefreq.

Do you send every URL to IndexNow on each deploy?

No. Only pages modified today go out. The full list (--all) is meant to be sent once, right after registering the site with Naver Search Advisor, the webmaster console of the Korean search engine Naver.

item.description:
CarDrawer 차서랍

Android app for used-car dealers in Korea

Recruiting 5 pilot shopsClosed testing on Google Play soon

One drawer
per car.

AI files every receipt and flags what's missing.

Snap a receipt, invoice or inspection report, or share a PDF. CarDrawer pulls out the vendor, amount, date and plate as suggestions and files them in that car's drawer. Every morning it shows what is due today, which papers are missing, which costs need approval and which cars have started losing money.

Apply for the pilot How it works

Free cost sheet template (CSV) · A per-car cost sheet that opens in Excel: 18 cost items with total-cost and difference formulas. No sign-up or email needed.

  • AI only suggests. A person confirms.
  • We never ask for your HeyDealer, Encar or other platform passwords.
  • Your costs are visible only to you and the people you allow.
The problem

Costs leak car by car, and papers scatter across chat rooms

Receipts in drawers and chats

Transport, polish, body work, dealer fees, listing ads: one car collects close to ten cost items. Matching each receipt to the right car falls on the office manager.

Deadlines in someone's head

Ownership transfer, inspection-report validity and platform claim windows differ for every car. Missing one means fines or disputes.

Profit known only after the sale

Financing interest and late invoices can turn a car you thought was profitable into a loss, and it is hard to see where each car stands today.

A car bought for ₩30.01M: about ₩630,000 left if sold in 3 months · cut the price in month 7 and it becomes a ₩970,000 loss

A dealer's public cost sheet (9 cost items; re-listing, interest and re-inspection added in month 7). Source: Clien post, 23 Aug 2025 (Korean), checked Oct 2026. One case, not a general figure.
What it does

Snap it, it sticks. Missing pieces come first.

  • Snap and it sticks

    “Snap the receipt. We attach it to the right car.”

    Upload from the camera, gallery or share menu in three taps. AI suggests the vendor, amount, date and plate; only values checked against the original reach your costs.

  • Today's deadlines, cars losing money

    “Do you know how much this car still makes?”

    The first screen gathers overdue tasks, today's deadlines, pending approvals and at-risk cars, with legal, platform and in-house deadlines labelled separately.

  • One shop, your costs stay yours

    “You decide who sees what.”

    Owner, buyers and office staff share the same car cards. Purchase prices, costs and counterparties are visible only with permission, and access ends the moment someone leaves.

  • Works next to your apps

    “Keep your apps. We fill the gaps.”

item.title: Block puzzle difficulty tuned with simulation bots – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · How-to

Block puzzle difficulty: how simulation bots caught a game you could never lose

If every tray of three pieces is guaranteed to fit, a player who finds each tray's solution never loses. Block Turn now keeps that guarantee for the first 10 trays only.

As first specified, the classic mode of Block Turn had no game over. We found out from bots, not players: on October 3, 2026, under the supply rule written in the spec (v1), a bot that plans the whole tray played 80 games, and all 80 hit the 3,000-move cap. The shipped rule, v7, ends a planner's game after a median of 122 moves and a greedy bot's after 47.

Numbers come from the sugar-game repository: the supply experiment log (docs/block/lab.md, measured 2026-10-03), the spec review, and the engine code and tests. Checked on October 19, 2026.

One friendly promise removed the game over

Block Turn is an 8×8 block puzzle in the Block Blast mold: you get three pieces, place them, full rows and columns clear, and then you get three more. The spec we started from (v2.0) promised this in section 7.1: "When a new set of three pieces is dealt, there is at least one order in which all three fit on the current board." It was meant to answer players who feel the piece supply is rigged. The spec even added that a player can still get stuck by placing badly.

That caveat only covers weak play. For a player who finds the solution, the promise turns into a loop:

  1. When a tray arrives, some order places all three pieces.
  2. Play that order and the tray is empty.
  3. The next tray gets the same guarantee. Back to step 1.

The run never ends. Nothing in that argument depends on piece weights, so dealing more awkward pieces cannot break it. The bots confirmed that too (v3 and v4 below).

A greedy bot and a planning bot on the same seeds

The engine stores the board as a single 64-bit integer, so scoring a position takes a handful of bit operations. That speed is what made the planning bot practical.

  • Greedy bot: it scores every legal move right now with the formula below and plays the best one. A cleared line is worth 10, so it usually picks the move that clears the most lines.
  • Planning bot: it searches every order and placement of the pieces left in the tray, plays the first move of the best plan, and searches again on the next move.

Both use the same board score:

score = lines cleared × 10 − 3 × holes − 0.3 × filled cells + 2 × room
holes = empty cells boxed in on all four sides
room  = is there space for a 3×3 square, a 1×4 bar, a 4×1 bar (0–3)

In the final comparison each supply version got 160 greedy games and 80 planner games, and every version used the same seeds. A game stops at 3,000 moves. The bots are not models of people. We assume a person lands somewhere between them, and we use the bot numbers only to rank supply rules against each other.

The four numbers that decided it

  • Planner games that hit the 3,000-move cap. Anything above zero rejects the version, because it means the game cannot be lost.
  • Planner median divided by greedy median. In a high-score mode, "play better, last longer" is most of the fun, so we wanted skill to show up as run length.
  • Greedy run length, so a careless player doesn't wash out in a few trays.
  • Tray generation time at p95, to see whether supply cost matters on a phone.

Supply rules v1 to v7, side by side

The awkward pieces are the 3×3 square, the 2×3 rectangle in both orientations and the four-cell bar in both orientations. "Pressure" means that every N moves those pieces gain one more multiple of their base weight, up to a cap.

VersionSupply ruleGreedy medianPlanner medianPlanner games at capOutcome
v1The spec: every tray fully placeable56 moves3,000 moves80/80Rejected
v2v1, plus 3× weight for pieces of 3 cells or fewer when fewer than 28 cells are emptyNot in the results tableDropped (made the game easier)
v3v1 plus pressure every 30 moves, up to 5×Not in the results table60/60Rejected
v4v1 plus pressure every 20 moves, up to 8×Not in the results table60/60Rejected
v5v7 plus pressure every 30 moves, up to 5×44 moves80 moves0A/B candidate
v6v7 plus pressure every 20 moves, up to 8×44 moves82 moves0Not used
v7Full guarantee for the first 10 trays, then only "at least one piece fits"47 moves122 moves0Default

Under v1 the planner's median game lasted 1,001 trays and scored 26,772 points. Under v7 it was 41 trays and 998 points. In the four versions with full numbers (v1, v5, v6, v7), the greedy bot never reached the cap.

We picked v7 for the skill gap: 122 moves against 47 is 2.6×. Adding pressure (v5, v6) cut that gap to 1.8 to 1.9×, mostly by cutting the strong player's runs short. Shorter runs mean more game-over screens, but they also mean a good player gets less for being good. So v7 shipped as the default, and v5 is parked as an A/B candidate.

Supply cost turned out to be a non-issue. Tray generation stayed at or under 0.2 ms at p95 for every version with timings in the table, and the spec's last-resort fallback (deal three single cells) never fired in 2,710 trays of the earlier Python simulation.

If a game spec says the player can "always" do something, run a bot that exploits that promise to the end before you build on it. Reading the sentence will not show you the problem.

The AI's first review pushed the other way

Earlier the same day, the spec review written by our AI coding agent had already simulated the supply rule in Python. It ran a random bot and a one-move greedy bot for 150 games each, with medians of 17 and 26 moves. It also tried a bot that reads the whole tray, then gave up on it: searching a single tray on an empty board took more than ten minutes in Python.

From those short runs, the review concluded that a solvable tray does not guarantee a long game, and recommended "relief" supply: deal smaller pieces when the board gets crowded. That is v2 in the table. The real problem was the opposite one.

The mistake was structural. A promise that only matters to the strongest player had been tested with the weakest bots. Once the Kotlin engine existed, the planning bot ran in reasonable time and every v1 planner game hit the cap. v2 was dropped, and spec v2.1 rewrote the supply promise as v7. The engine, the experiment tool and the tests landed together in commit cd62087 (October 4, 2026, Korea time).

(The Python greedy bot used a different board score with no "room" term, so its 26 moves and the Kotlin greedy bot's 56 under v1 are not a like-for-like comparison.)

The v1 finding is pinned by a unit test, a planner cannot be stopped under the full guarantee: on 20 seeds, playing each tray's solution must pass 300 moves.

What we still have to check

  • We don't know how long a human run is yet. The target is a median of 60 to 150 moves (roughly 4 to 10 minutes), and if real runs fall outside it we switch to v5. The end-of-run event that carries the move count, post_score, had fired only twice in total as of our October 17 GA4 review. The same review noted that the first-run flow never showed classic mode, so commit d1f6de1 (1.1.2) added a button into classic mode after the last tutorial.
  • Since 1.1.4 (b2d305d, October 17) a classic run allows two revives. The supply experiment ran without revives, so run length with revives needs measuring again.
  • The default supply rule itself is pinned by a test (default supply guarantees the first ten trays fully and never deals a dead tray after), so switching the default back to v1 would fail it. What no test checks is that a planner actually loses before the cap under the default supply. Today only a fresh supply experiment run shows that.

How the earlier apps came out of the same agent-driven workflow is in How we shipped four Android apps in 20 days with an AI coding agent.

FAQ

What should the game over condition be in a block puzzle?

The game ends when none of the remaining pieces fits anywhere. If the supply only ever deals trays that fully fit, a strong player never meets that condition. Block Turn guarantees full trays for the first 10 and, after that, only that at least one piece fits.

Can't you fix it by dealing more hard pieces?

No. Even with awkward pieces weighted up to 8× (v4), every planner game reached the 3,000-move cap. While the full guarantee stands, weights only change which solvable tray you get.

How many games does a balance simulation need?

In the final comparison we ran 160 greedy and 80 planner games per version, on the same seeds for every version (the earlier v3 and v4 runs used 60 planner games). That was enough to separate results like 80/80 games at the cap versus 0/80.

item.title: VIBRATE crash and the fresh-install monkey test – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Incident

The agent said it was tested. The game crashed on the first tutorial tap: a missing VIBRATE permission and the fresh-install monkey test

Scripted device tests missed a crash caused by one missing permission line. Running adb monkey on a freshly cleared app reproduced it at the 15th of 800 events.

At 22:58 on October 1, 2026 (Korea time), our AI coding agent installed a pre-release build of the puzzle game Arrow Knots on a Galaxy S24 and reported "launched in 857 ms, no crash". Four minutes later the operator reported that it errored out in the tutorial: the app closed on the first arrow tap. The code called Vibrator.vibrate, the manifest did not declare android.permission.VIBRATE, and the call threw a SecurityException. The fix, commit 65dcf41, landed 5 minutes 29 seconds after the crash report, and a fresh-install monkey script (f7beb3d) followed 15 seconds later.

Sources: the game repository's git history, the agent's session log from that night, and the agent's memory files. Times are Korea Standard Time (UTC+9). Checked on October 19, 2026.

Four minutes from "installed" to "it crashes"

TimeWhat happened
22:47Commit 3eb21df adds the tutorial and switches haptics to VibrationEffect composition primitives
22:58Agent reports the S24 install as "no crash". The S24 then drops off adb, so no screenshot. Asked "So is it tested?", it says the S24 was only installed and launched, and the S21 had "automated tests complete"
23:02Operator: it errors out in the tutorial. On the S21, with progress cleared, monkey seed 7 crashes the app at event 15 of 800
23:07Fix committed as 65dcf41; tools/monkey_check.sh follows 15 seconds later as f7beb3d

The agent's mistake was in what "no crash" rested on: am start -W returning Status: ok and a 857 ms launch time. Nothing on screen was ever tapped, and tapping was exactly what killed the app. (The logcat it read did contain a FATAL EXCEPTION, from a Samsung system app on September 30. The agent correctly ignored it. It checked carefully, just the wrong thing.)

Cause: Vibrator.vibrate without the VIBRATE permission

Ten minutes before the install, commit 3eb21df replaced View.performHapticFeedback with Vibrator.vibrate(VibrationEffect.startComposition()…). The code comment gives the reason: on Samsung devices CONTEXT_CLICK is barely felt. It was a game-feel change.

The two APIs have different rules. View haptics need no permission. Vibrator.vibrate needs android.permission.VIBRATE, and the manifest did not declare it. The game buzzes every time an arrow leaves the board, so the very first tutorial tap was the crash.

E AndroidRuntime: FATAL EXCEPTION: main
E AndroidRuntime: Process: (pre-release package name), PID: 12034
E AndroidRuntime: java.lang.SecurityException: vibrate: Neither user 10322 nor current process has android.permission.VIBRATE.

The fix touched two files, six lines added and one removed: declare the permission, and fall back to view haptics if the vibrator call fails for any reason.

<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.VIBRATE" />
runCatching { v.vibrate(VibrationEffect.startComposition().addPrimitive(primitive, scale).compose()) }
    .onFailure { view.performHapticFeedback(fallback) }

VIBRATE is a normal permission, granted at install with no dialog. Leave it out and the debug build still compiles. Nothing visible warns you.

Why the scripted tests missed it

Two device scripts were running on the S21 at the time. tutorial_check.py taps the three tutorial lessons in a fixed order. device_check.py writes a progress file to jump to a given level, then solves the board. Neither had a real pass condition. The tutorial script stops only if it cannot find the "Next" button, and the level script prints how many taps it sent. Neither looked for a crash in logcat or checked that the process was still alive.

The agent's own explanation was that the scripts only tap a fixed path. That is half right. The bigger hole was a check that never looked at crashes. (The tutorial script did run to the end on the S21 at about 22:45. Whether that build already had the vibration change was not checked that night, and the log does not say.)

device_check.py also writes tutorialDone=true when it jumps to a level, so it skips the first screens a new player sees by design. The new-player path only exists when the app has no data.

The fresh-install monkey script

tools/monkey_check.sh loops over three fixed seeds (7, 21, 99). For each one it wipes the app's data, launches it, sends 800 random events, and counts FATAL EXCEPTION lines in logcat. Any non-zero count fails the run. Below is the core of the current version, without device selection, output cleanup and the exit code. The script defaults to the debug package; here it uses the release package published on Play.

PKG=com.sugarmount.arrows
adb shell setprop debug.firebase.analytics.app $PKG
for seed in 7 21 99; do
  adb shell am force-stop $PKG
  adb shell pm clear $PKG
  adb logcat -c
  adb shell am start -W -n $PKG/sugar.arrows.MainActivity
  sleep 2
  adb shell monkey -p $PKG --pct-touch 90 --pct-motion 10 --pct-nav 0 --pct-majornav 0 \
    --pct-syskeys 0 --pct-appswitch 0 --throttle 120 -s $seed 800
  n=$(adb logcat -d | grep -c "FATAL EXCEPTION")
  echo "seed=$seed fatal=$n"
done
  • -p keeps events inside this package.
  • --pct-touch 90 --pct-motion 10: 90% taps, 10% drags. Navigation, system keys and app switching are set to 0 so the run stays in the game.
  • --throttle 120 waits 120 ms between events. The last argument, 800, is the event count, so a run takes at least 96 seconds.
  • -s fixes the seed, which replays the same event sequence. Before the fix, seed 7 printed System appears to have crashed at event 15 of 800 using seed 7. After it, the same seed injected all 800.

"Fresh install" here means no app data at all. The first version deleted a single progress file through run-as, which only works on debuggable builds. When release signing went in on October 3 (commit f421333), it became pm clear, with the comment "works on release (non-debuggable) builds too". If you suspect the install itself, run adb uninstall and install again. The script does not reinstall per seed; it clears data.

The pass condition changed too. The first version counted every FATAL EXCEPTION on the device, which also counts other apps' crashes, like the Samsung one on the S24. On October 4 the block puzzle game's block_monkey.sh (commit 575aaa1) began counting only Process: <package>, lines plus am_anr entries from the events buffer. Its comment notes that uiautomator and the monkey tool can die on their own. On October 18 (dca02f2) both scripts gained a setprop debug.firebase.analytics.app call before the loop, so test runs land in Firebase DebugView instead of the GA4 reports.

(During the post-fix check, the S21 briefly disconnected in the middle of seed 21. Any run that printed - waiting for device - was thrown out and repeated.)

The rule: no "done" without a fresh-install monkey run

After that night the agent's memory gained one rule. Before calling an Android build tested, run monkey_check.sh on the connected device, on top of the fixed-path scripts, and name every device it ran on. Always run it when the manifest, a permission or a system-service call changes. The rule also says it plainly: installing is not verifying.

Commit messages changed after that. As of October 19, 2026, 19 of the 144 commits since f7beb3d mention monkey in the message, and 16 of those report a result, in lines like "release (R8, test ads) monkey 3x1500 0 fatals" and "Android 7 launch and monkey pass on API 24". The other three are a tool list or a "still to run". Reported event counts range from 600 to 4,000.

When an agent says "done", ask which device and what ran on it. Without a monkey result from clean app data, we do not accept it as done. The wider pre-release routine is in What to check before shipping an AI-built Android app, and how we pin rules like this one for the agent is in How to write AGENTS.md for an AI coding agent.

Monkey runs are not the whole answer. The next day (October 2) a new stress suite crashed the game 28 times on its first pass through 300 levels: a blocked arrow springing back from far away overshot and read points[-1], an IndexOutOfBoundsException fixed in 69781a7. A fresh-install monkey run starts at the tutorial and the first level, so deep levels need their own runs.

What is still open

Arrow Knots' monkey_check.sh still counts every FATAL EXCEPTION on the device and ignores ANRs. It should match the block game's script and count only its own process's crashes plus ANRs. Several agent sessions share the same phones, so another app's crash failing our run is the first thing to fix.

FAQ

Do I need to ask the user for the VIBRATE permission?

No. VIBRATE is a normal permission, granted at install once it is declared in AndroidManifest.xml. View.performHapticFeedback works without it, but calling Vibrator.vibrate without the declaration throws a SecurityException and kills the app.

How many seeds and events should an adb monkey run use?

Our default is three seeds (7, 21, 99) at 800 events each, and five commits record release builds with test ads run at 1,500 events per seed. Fixing the seed is what lets you replay the exact sequence that failed.

Can I run monkey on a build with live ads?

We never do. Random taps on real ads are invalid clicks and put the AdMob account at risk, so monkey and other automated taps only run on builds using Google's test ad IDs.

If unit tests pass, can I skip the monkey run?

Not if you want to catch this kind of crash. All 31 engine unit tests passed that night. Permission checks happen in the device's system service, so a JVM unit test never sees them.

Building an Android HWP viewer: rhwp in a WebView, measured on 222 documents

Running the open-source rhwp engine inside an Android WebView, 221 of 222 Korean HWP and HWPX files opened on a Galaxy S21, with a median of 1.2 to 1.5 seconds from tap to first page.

221 of 222 Korean word-processor files opened. Before writing HWP Viewer SugarDoc, we wanted to know whether the engine could carry an app at all, so on October 3, 2026 we opened every file from a cold start on a Galaxy S21 (Android 15, WebView 153). The engine passed, with two catches. Drawing every page of a 384-page file pushed the WebView renderer to 2.8 GB, and the set the first report called "24 government documents" held only 17 real government attachments.

Numbers come from the engine spike report in SugarMount's app repository (sugar-utils; measured 2026-10-03, commit 7b0e567), the follow-up verification report (2026-10-05), and a recount from the raw result JSON done while writing this note. Checked on October 19, 2026.

HWP, HWPX and why a viewer is hard

HWP is the file format of Hancom Office Hangul, the word processor that Korean government offices, schools and many employers still use. HWP 5 is a binary compound file; HWPX is the newer ZIP-and-XML version; very old files are HWP 3.0. On a phone they usually arrive as attachments in KakaoTalk (Korea's main messenger) or email.

Layout is the hard part. Government press releases lean on dense tables, logos and fixed line breaks, and exam papers add equations and two-column pages. A viewer that gets the text but breaks the tables is useless for these.

Setup: one phone, 222 files, a cold start each time

rhwp is an open-source HWP/HWPX parser written in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly. It renders each page as SVG and is MIT-licensed. We used the npm package @rhwp/core 0.8.6, and the shipped app is still pinned to that version.

The test app was a single WebView with rhwp and the font stylesheet rhwp ships (153 font rules). For every file the app was force-stopped and relaunched; the first three pages went into the DOM and the rest were only timed.

  • Attachments from Korea's government policy portal, korea.kr: 17 files downloaded on 2026-10-02 (14 press releases; 13 HWPX, 4 HWP).
  • 198 samples from the rhwp repository, each with a reference PDF printed from Hancom Office 2020 or 2022, so page counts and first-page images can be compared. Many are hard cases: exam papers, equations, converted HWP 3.0 files.
  • Seven more files, explained in the section on what the AI got wrong.

We had no low-end phone. There are no numbers here for 3 to 4 GB RAM devices.

Results: 221 of 222 opened

"Tap to first page" is app launch time plus first-page render time, so it includes the cold start. p90 is the value where the slowest 10% begin. Renderer memory is the PSS (proportional set size: private memory plus a fair share of shared pages) of the WebView renderer process.

Metrickorea.kr, 17 filesFirst report's "24 government documents"rhwp samples, 198
Opened17/1724/24197/198
Tap to first page, median1.4 s1.5 s1.2 s
Tap to first page, p901.6 s2.1 s1.9 s
Tap to first page, max1.8 s3.0 s3.3 s
Render per page, median-10 ms6 ms
Renderer memory (PSS), max286 MB391 MB422 MB

The one failure, issue2063_huge_cellbreak_table.hwp, is a stress test built around a giant table split across pages; it ran past the 120-second limit. The spike report made a fallback path a condition for adopting the engine, and the app now lets you keep waiting or hand the file to another app after 10 seconds.

Fidelity held up. Against the reference PDFs, page counts matched for 195 of 197 samples (the other two were one page off), and the median first-page image similarity was 0.997. We also put seven files (two press releases, five samples) side by side with Hancom's output. The press-release tables, logos and bold text and the exam paper's equations and two columns looked nearly the same. The one visible miss was the first question number, "문1)", dropped from one exam paper.

A 384-page file only works if you draw the visible pages

One rhwp sample is a 384-page government administration handbook (10.7 MB). With every page's SVG in the DOM, the WebView renderer process grew to 2.8 GB. Drawing only the visible pages, the same file sat at 255 MB in one run and 366 MB in another run the same afternoon. Read it as an order of magnitude, not a precise figure.

If you build an HWP viewer on a WebView, put virtual scrolling (only the visible pages and their neighbours in the DOM) in from day one. Do not plan to add it later.

The shipped viewer gives every page an empty slot of the right size and keeps SVG only for the visible pages plus two on each side, or one on each side on low-memory devices. Rendered SVG strings live in a byte-capped LRU (least recently used) cache, so the pages viewed longest ago are dropped first.

Fonts went from 144 MB to 9.2 MB

The font folder that comes with rhwp is 87 files and 144,327,972 bytes. The spike report called it "138 MB", which is the same number counted in mebibytes. The 222 documents actually used 17 of those files, about 37 MB.

The app ships 10 files, 9,207,952 bytes, about 6% of the original. Two rules decided what went in: a clear license and a close look. Hancom's own Hamchorom fonts were left out because Hancom's license page does not spell out whether they may be bundled in an app; Hamchorom Batang is drawn with Noto Serif KR and Hamchorom Dotum with NanumGothic, both under the SIL Open Font License. rhwp's NanumGothic was a subset that kept the reserved font name, so we swapped in the original TTF from google/fonts.

On 2026-10-05 we measured the cost on the same S21: how much first-page ink overlap (F1) against the reference drops with the substitute fonts. The pass mark, fixed in advance, was a median drop of 0.02 or less; the median came out at 0.0071. One file went over at 0.0336, a college entrance exam (Suneung) paper whose title is in Chinese characters (hanja). The difference sat in the hanja title and the circled numbers ① to ⑤, which the bundled fonts lack, so the system font draws them.

What the AI got wrong, and what verification changed

An AI coding agent (Claude) session ran the engine spike and wrote its report. Two days later, the follow-up experiments split the work: one agent measured, a separate verifier agent reopened the evidence files and recomputed every number, and only corrected values went into the docs. The first report's statistics were recounted at that point.

First reportAfter verification
24 real government documents17 korea.kr files (14 press releases) plus 7 others: 4 byte-identical to samples, 3 rhwp test fixtures
Samples: 177 HWP, 21 HWPX180 HWP, 18 HWPX (9 of them HWP 3.0)
Number recall around 0.9A bug in the comparison script: text runs were joined with no separator, so 11:00 and 10. 2. became 11:0010. 2.. Fixed, all 17 korea.kr files score 1.0 (a lenient upper bound)
Bundled fonts 9,700 KB (the follow-up's measuring agent)KiB written as KB; 9,933,636 bytes is 9.93 MB (later cut to 9,207,952 bytes)

The first row stung. "24 of 24 government documents" reads well, and 7 of the 24 were not government documents. That is why the results table has a separate korea.kr column. Counted alone, the 17 real files were faster (1.4 s median) and lighter (286 MB max). The engine decision did not change, but without the verifier we would have published a number with the wrong provenance.

Writing this note, we recomputed the medians once more from the raw s21b.json. The report's 1.5, 2.1 and 3.0 seconds came out exactly; the 366 MB run of the 384-page file turned up then. (The verification report also flagged that another script had overwritten one raw file, which must be regenerated before anyone quotes it.)

Still open

  • Low-end phones. According to the development plan, the Firebase Test Lab low-end run has not happened yet, so we do not know how a 400 MB renderer behaves on a 3 to 4 GB phone.
  • Hanja-heavy documents. The bundled fonts have no hanja and the system font draws them; the 0.0336 is recorded as that cost, from a sample of two.
  • Upgrading rhwp. It is pre-1.0, so the app pins 0.8.6 and every build checks that the engine files match the pinned copy. An upgrade will be re-measured on the same 222 files. The other pre-release checks are in What to check before shipping an AI-built Android app.

FAQ

Can rhwp be used in a commercial Android app?

Yes. rhwp is MIT-licensed, but the Rust crates compiled into its WASM (Apache-2.0, BSD and others) need their notices too. The fonts it ships carry their own licenses and need checking file by file. HWP Viewer SugarDoc bundles 10 font files with confirmed licenses, OFL and others, and leaves out Hamchorom.

Why does a WebView HWP viewer use so much memory?

Every rendered page stays in the DOM as SVG. A 384-page file took the renderer to 2.8 GB with all pages drawn and 255 MB with only the visible ones, so draw one or two pages around the screen and drop the rest.

Does one engine open both HWP and HWPX?

Yes. rhwp 0.8.6 opens both, and 221 of the 222 mixed files here opened. The difference between the two formats is explained in HWP vs HWPX: what differs and how to open both.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

More AX notes

  • androidx.pdf beta01 runs your Application.onCreate a second time, in an isolated process, and the PDF silently never opens
  • Jetpack Compose splits Korean between syllables, but the stacked 'R/u/l/e' label came from how a Row measures
  • Play Console said our DEX was 39% optimized. The culprit was a keep rule for an SDK we never used
  • 84 agents reviewed a release: three refuters per finding, and only the 20 survivors got fixed
  • Our contrast checker passed while skipping 40% of the text: make it print how much it measured
  • "Use hundreds of agents" in practice: 10 workstreams, 59 commits in a day, three running at once

item.title: Convert an HWP file to PDF on Android – SugarMount
item.description:
Help · Android

Convert an HWP file to PDF on Android

Open the HWP or HWPX file in HWP Viewer SugarDoc, tap ⋮ (More options) and then Save as PDF, and pick a folder. The PDF is made on your phone without uploading the document. Long documents are cut to the first 15 pages.

This guide is based on HWP Viewer SugarDoc 1.2.0, an Android app made by SugarMount. The Save as PDF menu item arrived in 1.2.0; on older versions use the print screen instead (see below). The screenshots show the app in Korean.

Without an app, and the catch

HWP and HWPX are Korean word-processor formats, and Android phones usually have no app that opens them. If the phone cannot open the file, it cannot print it to PDF either, so the app-free options are all off the phone:

  • Ask the sender for a PDF. They export it from the program that made it, so the layout matches best. You have to wait for a reply.
  • Save as PDF in a desktop HWP program. Good for long documents where layout matters. Needs a computer with the program.
  • Upload to a web converter. Nothing to install, but the file goes to that site's server. Avoid it for letters or forms with names, phone numbers or addresses.

Save as PDF in HWP Viewer SugarDoc

  1. Open the document — tap the HWP or HWPX file in KakaoTalk, email or your file manager and choose HWP Viewer from Open with or Share, or pick it with Find in my files inside the app.
  2. ⋮ → Save as PDF — tap ⋮ at the top right of the document and choose Save as PDF.
  3. Check the page notice — if the document is longer than the limit, the app tells you how many pages will be saved first. Tap Save to go on or Cancel to stop without making a file.
  4. Pick where to save — Android's save screen opens with the document's name plus .pdf filled in. Choose a folder and tap Save.
  5. Done — the message "Saved as a PDF." appears. The HWP or HWPX file you received is not changed.

Checked on a Galaxy S21 (Android 15) with the SugarDoc 1.2.0 release build on October 18, 2026: a 47-page HWP document showed the notice and produced a 15-page PDF, and a 3-page HWPX document was saved with all 3 pages.

Save through the print screen

Tap Print in the ⋮ menu to open Android's print screen (on versions before 1.2.0 the item is called Print or save as PDF). Under Select printer, choose the save-as-PDF option (its name varies by phone) to keep the result as a PDF file. Use this if Save as PDF fails; the same page limit applies.

"In Android 4.4 (API level 19) and higher, the framework provides services for printing images and documents directly from Android applications."

Source: Android Developers, Printing content

Which way to use

MethodPhone onlyUploadLengthUse it when
SugarDoc Save as PDFYesNoneFirst 15 pages (6 on low-memory phones)You need a short notice or letter as a PDF right now
SugarDoc Print → PDFYesNoneSame as aboveSave as PDF failed, or you are on a version before 1.2.0 (there the item is ‘Print or save as PDF’)
Ask the senderYes (you wait)NoneNo limitThe layout must match, or it is longer than 15 pages
Desktop HWP programNoNoneDepends on the programYou need to edit a long document first
Web converterYesTo their serverVaries by siteThe document has no personal information

Verdict: for a document of 15 pages or fewer that you need as a PDF now, Save as PDF in the app is the quickest. For longer documents or forms where layout matters, get a PDF from the sender or make it on a computer.

Limits and what to do when it fails

  • Only the first pages are saved. Usually the first 15, or the first 6 on phones with little memory. You cannot choose a page range.
  • Distribution-only documents cannot be saved. When printing and copying are locked, Save as PDF and Print do not appear in the menu.
  • PDF files have no Save as PDF. They are already PDFs, so only Print is offered, and a password-protected PDF cannot be printed.
  • Layout may differ slightly. If the original fonts are not on your phone, similar fonts are used, so line breaks and spacing can shift. Open the saved PDF and check it before you submit it anywhere.
  • If it will not open, it will not save. Documents locked by a company DRM program cannot be opened. If the file does not open at all, start with what to check when an HWPX file will not open.
  • No PDF-to-HWP. SugarDoc is a viewer only.

About the HWP format

HWP is the native format of the Hancom word processor widely used in Korea. Its specification is public, which is why other apps can read it. Hancom says (in Korean) that it published the HWP binary format and the HWPML markup language on June 29, 2010: "한컴은 2010년 6월 29일에 자사의 바이너리 포맷인 HWP와 마크업 언어인 HWPML을 공개하였습니다."

Source: Hancom download center, HWP and OWPML formats. For how .hwp and .hwpx differ, see HWP vs HWPX.

FAQ

Does saving as PDF cost anything?

No. Save as PDF and Print need no payment, and the app has no ads.

Is my document uploaded anywhere?

No. SugarDoc does not send documents to a server; the PDF is made on your phone. See the HWP Viewer SugarDoc privacy policy.

Where is the saved PDF?

In the folder you picked on the save screen. The folder shown first can differ by phone, so check its name before you tap Save. Afterwards you can find the PDF in your phone's Files app.

Can I convert a document longer than 15 pages in full?

Not in SugarDoc. Only the first 15 pages (6 on low-memory phones) are saved. For the whole document, ask the sender for a PDF or make it on a computer.

If I cancel on the save screen, is an empty file left behind?

No. Cancelling on the save screen creates no file.

item.title: HWP vs HWPX: what differs and how to open both – SugarMount
item.description:
Help · Android

HWP vs HWPX: what differs and how to open both

HWP and HWPX are both Korean Hangul documents, but they are built differently, so renaming the file does not convert it. On an Android phone, open both with one viewer; converting HWPX to HWP needs the Hangul word processor on a PC.

This article uses SugarMount's Android app HWP Viewer SugarDoc (SugarDoc for short; shown as "HWP Viewer" on your phone). It cannot convert HWPX to HWP or HWP to HWPX. Editing (Pro) covers body and table cell text in HWP documents only; HWPX documents cannot be edited yet.

How HWP and HWPX differ

.hwp is the long-standing format of Hancom's Hangul word processor, common in Korean schools, offices and government. It is a binary compound file, so its contents are not human-readable. .hwpx is the newer open format (OWPML): the document is written as XML files packed into one ZIP archive.

Hancom states which versions support each format:

"HWP의 개방형 문서 형식인 OWPML은 HWP 2018 버전부터 ".owpml" 확장자로 지원하고 있으며, 하위 버전은 HWP 2010 버전부터 ".hwpx" 확장자로 지원하고 있습니다."

In English: OWPML, HWP's open document format, is supported with the ".owpml" extension from HWP 2018, and with the ".hwpx" extension from HWP 2010. The same page describes the .hwp 5.x format as the one used from HWP 2002 through HWP 2018. Source: Hancom Download Center, HWP/OWPML format (Korean, checked October 18, 2026).

So the same letter can arrive in either format. An app that reads only one of them cannot open the other, and changing the extension leaves the inside unchanged.

Side by side

Item.hwp.hwpx
Inside the fileBinary compound fileXML files in a ZIP (OWPML)
Hangul word processor support (per Hancom)5.x format from HWP 2002From HWP 2010
Rename the extensionDoes not work. The inside stays the same
Open in SugarDocYes, including old HWP 3.0Yes
Password-protectedOpens with the password. Password-protected HWP 3.0 files cannot be openedOpens with the password
Convert between them in SugarDocNo

Verdict: if you only need to read the document, the difference does not matter; one app that opens both is enough. The format only matters when you must send the file on to someone using a Hangul version older than HWP 2010. Then re-save it as .hwp on a PC, or send a PDF.

Without an app, and the limits

  • Renaming the file: does not work. A .hwpx renamed to .hwp is still a ZIP-based HWPX inside, so programs that cannot read HWPX still fail.
  • Re-saving in the Hangul word processor on a PC: the usual way to get .hwp. Open the file in a version that supports .hwpx, then save a copy and choose the .hwp file type. Menu names vary by version, and you need a PC with the program.
  • Asking the sender for another format: the most reliable. The author can re-save as .hwp or PDF with the fewest layout changes, but you have to wait for a reply.
  • Your phone's built-in apps: usually open neither. Android phones generally have a PDF viewer but no app for .hwp or .hwpx.

Open either format with SugarDoc

  1. Tap the file — In KakaoTalk, email or your file manager, tap the .hwp or .hwpx file and pick HWP Viewer from "Open with" or "Share". For a file already saved on the phone, use Find in my files in the app.
  2. Don't choose a format — There is nothing to pick. The app tells HWP, HWPX and PDF apart by reading the file's contents, not by the extension at the end of its name.
  3. Find it again later — Every document you open is listed with its format (HWP, HWPX or PDF). When the list grows, search by file name.
  4. Enter the password if asked — A password-protected HWP or HWPX file opens once you type its password. The password is not saved.

Screenshots are real app screens captured for SugarDoc's store listing. Menu names can differ slightly by app version and phone model.

What it cannot do

  • No format conversion. SugarDoc cannot turn HWPX into HWP or the other way round, and it cannot create documents. Editing (Pro) covers body and table cell text in HWP documents only.
  • You can keep a PDF. If the recipient has no Hangul word processor, or an old one, a PDF may be the easiest thing to send. See convert an HWP file to PDF on Android for the steps and page limits.
  • Layout may differ slightly. When the original font is not on your phone, a similar font is used, so line breaks and spacing can shift. Old HWP 3.0 files may differ more.
  • Some files will not open. DRM-protected documents, password-protected HWP 3.0 files and files over 1 GB cannot be opened. Distribution-only documents may not open, or show only a preview.
  • Other office formats are not supported. Excel, Word and PowerPoint files do not open.

If a file does not open at all, the cause is usually your phone's app settings rather than the format. Start with when an HWPX file won't open on your phone.

FAQ

If I rename .hwpx to .hwp, will it open?

No. Only the name changes; the file is still HWPX inside, so programs that cannot read HWPX still fail. To get a real .hwp, re-save it as .hwp in a Hangul word processor that supports .hwpx.

Can SugarDoc convert HWPX to HWP?

No. SugarDoc has no format conversion. It opens both formats, and you can keep the document as a PDF.

Which format should I ask for?

For reading, either is fine; an app that opens both shows them the same way. If you must forward the file to someone using a Hangul version older than HWP 2010, .hwp or PDF is safer.

Do very old HWP 3.0 files open?

Yes, SugarDoc opens them, though they may look more different from the original. Password-protected HWP 3.0 files cannot be opened.

Are my documents uploaded anywhere?

No. SugarDoc opens documents on your phone without uploading them, and it never changes the original file. See the privacy policy for details.

  • When an HWPX file won't open on your phone
  • Convert an HWP file to PDF on Android

item.title: How to open an HWPX or HWP file on Android – SugarMount
item.description:
Help · Android

How to open an HWPX or HWP file on Android

An HWPX or HWP file usually will not open on Android because the phone has no app for Korean word-processor documents. Install an HWP viewer, then choose it from Open with in KakaoTalk, email or your file manager.

This guide uses HWP Viewer SugarDoc, an Android app made by SugarMount; other HWP viewers work much the same way. Menu names vary a little by app version and phone. The screenshots are cropped from the app's Google Play screenshots of version 1.0.0.

Why the file will not open

  • No app can read it. Android phones usually come with something that opens PDFs, but nothing for .hwp or .hwpx. Tapping the file ends with a message that no app can open it.
  • The file arrives as an unknown type. Some apps hand over .hwpx as a generic file instead of a document, so a viewer you have installed may still be missing from the list of apps.
  • Another app is the default. If you once tapped Always for a different app, that app opens straight away without asking. If it cannot read HWPX you see a blank screen or an error.

HWPX is the newer of the two formats. Hancom, the maker of the Hangul word processor, says (in Korean) that its open format OWPML has been supported with the .hwpx extension since Hangul 2010:

"HWP의 개방형 문서 형식인 OWPML은 HWP 2018 버전부터 ".owpml" 확장자로 지원하고 있으며, 하위 버전은 HWP 2010 버전부터 ".hwpx" 확장자로 지원하고 있습니다."

Source: Hancom Download Center, HWP/OWPML format (Korean, checked October 18, 2026). The two formats are built differently; see HWP vs HWPX.

Without installing an app, and the catch

  • Ask the sender for a PDF. Every Android phone can show a PDF, and the layout matches the original best. You have to wait for a reply.
  • Open it on a computer with the Hangul word processor or another program that reads HWP. Not much help when you need the file on the go.
  • Upload it to a web viewer or converter. Nothing to install, but the document goes to that site's server. Avoid it for school letters, forms or anything with names, phone numbers or addresses.

When an HWP file from KakaoTalk will not open

  1. Install an HWP viewer — get an app that opens HWP and HWPX from Google Play. HWP Viewer SugarDoc shows no permission prompts after installing and needs no sign-up.
  2. Tap the file in the chat — tap the file in the KakaoTalk chat to download it.
  3. Open with another app — from the file screen's menu (⋮ or the share button) choose Open with another app, then pick HWP Viewer from the list. Tap Always if you do not want to choose every time.
  4. Go back when you are done — Back returns you to KakaoTalk. Documents you open collect under Received documents in the app, so you can find them later by file name without scrolling back through the chat.

The menu names and their place differ by KakaoTalk version and phone. The app's own home screen shows the same three steps under Open documents from KakaoTalk.

Files attached to an email

Tap the attachment in your mail app and a list of apps to open it with appears. Choose the HWP viewer there. If the mail app only downloads the file and shows no list, download it first and then use the steps in the next section. Each mail app shows attachments a little differently.

When the viewer is missing from the list

  1. Check the file-type setting — some apps send .hwpx without saying what kind of file it is. In HWP Viewer SugarDoc, Settings > Opening files > Show for all file types lets you pick the app even then. It is on by default; if you turned it off, turn it back on and tap the file again.
  2. Save the file to your phone — use Save or Download in the app you received it in. It usually goes to the Download folder.
  3. Pick it from inside the viewer — open HWP Viewer SugarDoc, tap Find in my files and choose the file. This uses Android's own file picker, so the app does not need access to all your storage.
  4. Or share it — if the app you received it in has Share, choose HWP Viewer from the share list.

When a different app opens instead

If another app opens with no list to choose from, that app is set as the default. Resize an ID photo for Korean application uploads

Check the site's rules first

Photo fields on Korean application, job and government sites usually set three separate conditions. Meeting one of them is not always enough.

  • File size: written as "500KB 이하" (500 KB or less). This is what the app fits.
  • Pixel size: for example 413 × 531 pixels. A fixed ratio means the photo must be cropped to it.
  • File type: usually JPG (JPEG). The app always saves JPEG.

The rules are in the notice or next to the upload button. For any site not covered here, follow that notice.

Without an app, and the limits

  • Ask the photo studio for a file: studios can often hand over a digital file sized for submission. This is the surest route, but you need to go back if the photo is already taken.
  • Your gallery app's editor: most Android gallery apps can crop, which handles the ratio. Menu names and resize options vary by phone and version, so we don't list them. After saving, check the real file size and pixels in the photo's details.
  • For a passport photo, the government resize tool: the Ministry of Foreign Affairs passport site has an online passport photo resize tool (Korean only). You upload a photo, zoom and move it until the face fits a red dotted guide, then save. It accepts JPG or PNG under 1 MB, and the page says the result is not for ID, half-size or visa photos.

Shrink it with Compress Image

The passport site lists the files it accepts for online renewal (quoted in Korean, our translation below):

"파일 크기 500KB 이하, 파일 형식 JPG/JPEG"

"휴대폰 등 모바일 기기로 촬영된 사진, 사진 편집 프로그램 등으로 과도한 보정을 한 사진은 여권 발급 시 사진이 실물과 다르게 표현될 수 있으므로 권장하지 않음"

Convert HEIC to JPG on a Samsung Galaxy phone

This article is based on Convert Image JPG PNG WEBP 1.0.3, an Android app made by SugarMount. If you want future photos saved as JPG from the start, read "Without an app" first.

HEIC vs JPG

HEIC is a file in the HEIF photo format, compressed with HEVC (H.265). JPG is far older, and almost every website, program and printer accepts it. That is why a HEIC photo that looks fine on your phone can be rejected by an upload form or fail to open on a PC.

Whether Android itself can read HEIC depends on the device. The supported formats table in the Android developer documentation says this about HEIF decoding:

"Android 9.0+ … Device optional. Check ImageDecoder.isMimeTypeSupported("image/heif") for 8-bit support. 10-bit decoding requires optional HEVC Main10 profile."

  • Turn off HEIF (high efficiency) saving in the camera — some phones have a camera setting for it. With it off, new photos are saved as JPG. The menu name and place vary by model and version. Photos you already took stay HEIC.
  • Conversion when sharing from the gallery — depending on the model, the gallery may have a setting that sends photos as JPG when you share them. It only applies to what you share, and may not leave a JPG file on the phone.
  • Convert on a PC — the PC program has to read HEIC, and you need to move the photos first.
  • Upload to a converter website — no install, but the photos go to that site's server. Avoid it for photos of faces, IDs or documents.

PNG to JPG on Android with a white background

JPG cannot store transparency, so converting a PNG to JPG fills its transparent areas with one solid colour. On Android, choose that colour in a converter app, set it to white, and save the result.

This guide uses SugarMount's Android app Convert Image JPG PNG WEBP (SugarConvert). Other converters work on the same principle: transparent areas always become a colour.

Without an app, and the catch

There are two common ways to convert without installing anything on the phone.

  • A web converter — upload the PNG in a browser and download a JPG. Nothing to install, but the image goes to that site's server. Not a good fit for IDs or documents, and the fill colour for transparent areas and the number of files per run vary by site.
  • An image editor on a computer — move the file to a PC and save it as JPEG. No upload, but you have to move files back and forth, and the colour transparent areas turn into depends on the program.

Either way, the JPG keeps no transparency. Check that the formerly transparent area is the colour you want.

Convert with the app

  1. Check the preset — on the home screen, make sure JPG for forms is selected: quality 90, transparent areas white. It is the default the first time you open the app.
  2. Pick the PNG files — tap Select photos or Pick from files. Use Pick from files to keep the original file names; the system photo picker does not share names, so those files are saved as SugarConvert plus the time. If a PNG has transparent areas, the Selected photos screen tells you they will be filled with the background colour. Tap Next.
  3. Choose the background colour — on Convert options, check that the output format is JPEG and pick White, Black or Gray under Transparent areas. Set quality between 40 and 100 (default 90) and check the preview.
  4. Create and save — tap Create results, compare the original and the result side by side, then tap Save all. Items whose transparency was filled are marked "transparent areas filled with white". Results are saved as new files in Pictures/SugarConvert; the original PNG stays as it was.

Screens are cropped from the store captures in the app's repository. Wording and layout may differ slightly between app versions.

Which method to use

MethodUploadColour for transparent areasSeveral files at onceVerdict
Web converterYes, to the site's serverVaries by siteVaries by siteFine for one or two non-sensitive images
Image editor on a PCNoVaries by programUsually one at a timeGood if the file is already on the PC
Convert Image appNo, converted on the deviceWhite, Black or Gray20 free, 100 with ProEasiest for several PNGs already on the phone

Why transparency turns into a colour

PNG can store how transparent each pixel is. The W3C PNG specification says:

“Indexed-color, greyscale, and truecolor images are supported, plus an optional alpha channel.”

Source: W3C, Portable Network Graphics (PNG) Specification (Third Edition). The alpha channel is the transparency data.

JPEG has no such data. The Android developer documentation notes it when describing how images are compressed and saved:

“JPEG only supports opaque pixels”

Source: Android Developers, Bitmap.compress().

So a PNG-to-JPG conversion has to decide what colour goes where the image was transparent. The app paints the chosen colour first and draws the image on top, so soft, semi-transparent edges blend into that colour. A PNG with no transparent areas converts the same whatever colour you pick.

  • Converting a JPG back to PNG does not restore lost detail or transparency, and the file may get larger.
  • Animated images are not converted; that item fails and the rest continue. Each image can be up to 50 MB and 50 MP.
  • No cropping or background removal. The only resize is shrinking the long edge.
  • Location and camera data (EXIF) are not copied to the result.

Does converting PNG to JPG lower the quality?

JPEG is lossy, so some detail is lost depending on the quality value. The default of 90 looks the same as the original for most photos; lower values give smaller files. The Results screen shows the real file sizes.

Can I fill transparency with black instead of white?

Yes. Pick Black or Gray under Transparent areas on the Convert options screen. Other colours are not available.

Will the JPG be smaller?

Photos with many colours usually get smaller, but simple graphics can get larger. If a result is larger than the original, the Results screen says so.

Where are the converted files saved?

As new files in the phone's Pictures/SugarConvert folder. The original PNG is not changed or deleted.

Are my images uploaded?

No. Conversion happens on the device and nothing is uploaded. See the Convert Image privacy policy for details.

Help · Android

Unmirror a selfie on a Samsung Galaxy phone

To fix a selfie you already took, flip it left to right and save it as a new photo. Google Photos does one picture at a time; the Flip & Rotate Image app's "Selfie as others see it" preset fixes a whole batch at once.

This article is based on Flip & Rotate Image 1.0.3, an Android app made by SugarMount. The screens below are store captures of version 1.0.0 with demo photos; the menus shown are the same in 1.0.3.

Why selfies look flipped

While you take a selfie, the front camera shows you a mirror image, so you see the face you know from the mirror. Other people see the opposite. The Android developer documentation describes the front-camera preview like this:

"Note that preview display of front-facing cameras is flipped horizontally before the rotation, that is, the image is reflected along the central vertical axis of the camera sensor. So the users can see themselves as looking into a mirror."

Source: Android Developers, Camera.setDisplayOrientation. This is the older camera API, but the mirrored preview works the same way.

Whether the saved photo keeps that mirror view or is stored the way others see you depends on the phone and its camera settings. Galaxy camera settings include a related option, but its name and location vary by model and software version, so we don't name it here. It applies to photos you take from then on; photos you already took stay as they are. Fix those with one of the methods below.

Without a new app, and the limits

If your phone has Google Photos, you can mirror one photo at a time in its editor. The Google Photos Help Center gives these steps:

  1. Open the photo in Google Photos and tap Edit at the bottom.
  2. Tap Crop, then Mirror.
  3. Tap the checkmark (Done), then choose Save or Save as copy.

"Save: Saves your changes to the original photo." "Save as copy: Makes a new photo with your edits without changes to the original."

Source: Google Photos Help, Edit your photos (Android)

Limits: one photo at a time. "Save" changes the original, so pick "Save as copy" if you want to keep it. Menu names can change between Google Photos versions. The Galaxy Gallery editor also differs by version, so we don't cover it here.

Fix many selfies at once with Flip & Rotate Image

  1. Tap "Selfie as others see it" — Under Quick start on the home screen, tap Selfie as others see it. It sets a left-right flip and opens the photo picker right away.
  2. Pick your selfies — Choose them in the Android photo picker: up to 20 at a time for free, 100 with Pro. Check the list and tap Next.
  3. Check the preview — The Transform screen lists "1 · Flip left ↔ right" under Applied in order. Compare the original with the preview and leave the output format on "Keep original". Tap Create results.
  4. Save and share — On the Results screen, compare the original and the result again, then tap Save all. The results go into the Pictures/SugarFlip folder as new files and the originals stay untouched. You can also tap Share.

The app applies the orientation your phone recorded in the photo (EXIF) first, so the flip follows the way the photo looks in your gallery. The same steps also turn an already unmirrored selfie back into the mirror view.

Methods compared

MethodPhotos already takenMany photosOriginalBest for
Change the camera settingNot changed——Choosing how future selfies are saved
Google Photos MirrorYesOne at a time"Save" changes it; "Save as copy" makes a new photoFixing one or two photos
Flip & Rotate Image, "Selfie as others see it"Yes20 free, 100 with ProAlways saved as a new file; original untouchedFixing a batch the same way at once

Verdict: for one or two photos, Google Photos' Mirror with "Save as copy" is quickest. For a batch of selfies from a trip or a party, Flip & Rotate Image is easier. To change future selfies, check your camera settings separately.

When it doesn't work, and limits

  • It doesn't change your camera settings. The app fixes photos you already took; new selfies are still saved the way your camera is set.
  • Photos only. Selfie videos and animated images (such as animated WebP) can't be flipped.
  • You can't send photos to it with Share from your gallery. Pick them inside the app with "Select photos" or a preset.
  • Photo details (EXIF) are not kept in the result. If you need the date or location, keep the original.
  • JPEGs are saved again at quality 95. The resolution stays the same, but the file isn't identical to the original and its size can change a little.
  • Each photo can be up to 50 MB and 50 megapixels.
  • Two left-right flips produce no result. They cancel out, and the app tells you so. Tap "Reset" under Applied in order and pick again.

FAQ

The text in my selfie is backwards. Will flipping fix it?

Yes. Backwards text means the photo was saved as a mirror image; flipping it left to right makes the text readable.

Will my original selfie be changed or deleted?

Flip & Rotate Image leaves the original alone and writes a new file to Pictures/SugarFlip. In Google Photos, "Save" changes the original, so choose "Save as copy".

Are my photos uploaded anywhere?

No. Flip & Rotate Image processes photos on your phone and doesn't upload them. See the Flip & Rotate Image privacy policy for details.

Does flipping lower the quality?

The resolution stays the same. JPEGs are saved again at quality 95, so the file isn't byte-for-byte identical. The Results screen shows the size before and after.

Can future selfies be saved the way others see me?

That is set in your phone's camera app. Flip & Rotate Image doesn't change camera settings.

Korean Christmas greeting card messages

A Korean Christmas greeting only needs one or two sentences that fit the person. You can send the words on their own, or use SugarCard to put them on a card and send it as an image or a snowfall video.

This guide is based on SugarCard 1.0.002, an Android app made by SugarMount. The app is in Korean. The example messages below were written for this page; the app has no built-in messages, so you type your own.

Example messages by recipient

Each line is Korean first, then what it means. Adding a name or one thing from this year makes it feel less formal. If the message goes on a card, two short lines read best.

Parents and family

  • 올 한 해도 늘 먼저 챙겨 주셔서 고마워요. 따뜻한 성탄절 보내세요.
  • Thank you for always looking after us this year. Have a warm Christmas.
  • 가족 모두 건강하게 한 해를 마무리할 수 있어서 감사한 성탄이에요.
  • I'm grateful we're all ending the year in good health. Merry Christmas.

Friends

  • 올해도 내 편 해 줘서 고마워. 즐거운 크리스마스 보내!
  • Thanks for being on my side again this year. Have a fun Christmas! (casual)
  • 바빠서 자주 못 봤지만 늘 생각했어. 연말에 꼭 얼굴 보자.
  • We were too busy to meet, but I thought of you. Let's catch up before the year ends. (casual)

Colleagues and clients

  • 한 해 동안 함께 일해 주셔서 감사합니다. 평안한 성탄절 보내시기 바랍니다.
  • Thank you for working with us this year. Wishing you a peaceful Christmas. (formal)
  • 성탄의 기쁨이 가정에 가득하시길 바랍니다. 내년에도 잘 부탁드립니다.

Teachers and elders

  • 선생님 덕분에 올 한 해 많이 배웠습니다. 행복한 성탄절 보내세요.
  • I learned a lot this year thanks to you. Have a happy Christmas. (polite)

Partner, or one short line

  • 올해 가장 좋은 선물은 너였어. 메리 크리스마스.

Without an app, and the limits

  • Text only — Edit an example above and send it. Fastest, but with no picture it blends into everyday chat.
  • A gallery photo plus text — Send your own photo and the message. They arrive as two separate messages, and the words are not on the picture.
  • A card image found online — Plenty to choose from, but someone may hold the rights, and you need an editing app to put text on it.

Send a Christmas card with SugarCard

  1. Pick Christmas — Tap the title at the top (for example 생생카드: 설날 ›) and choose 크리스마스 (Christmas). In November and December the app opens on Christmas.

  3. Type the message — Type in the box at the bottom and the text appears on the card right away in a handwriting-style font. Text colour and position are set per card.
  4. Tap send, then pick a format — The send button next to the box asks you to choose 눈 내리는 영상 (snowfall video) or 이미지로 공유 (share as image). The video is made on the phone, with a progress bar.
  5. Pick the app — Your phone's share screen opens. Choose KakaoTalk, Messages or another app.

That last screen is Android's own share screen. The Android developer documentation describes it like this:

"The Android Sharesheet is primarily designed for sending content outside your app or directly to another user."

So the list of apps you can send to depends on what is installed on your phone. Source: Android Developers, Send data to other apps
